title: What does Learning Look Like in Action - 2
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton begins to build a classroom-observable framework for learning by describing its first state, New learning. Four short portraits, a toddler with a shape box, a teenage guitarist, a hesitant philosophy student and a fashion student facing pattern making, show what the beginning of learning looks like. In every case it appears as hesitant, effortful struggle because the neuronal chain is fragile and the brain is spending energy. He distinguishes good struggling, which needs safety, challenge pitched correctly, time to practise and a worthwhile aim, from bad struggling. He argues teachers and leaders should treat struggle as the opening of learning, and recalls his own father's frustration over his maths.
points: New learning almost always looks like struggle, with hesitancy and uncertainty visible because nothing has yet become sticky.
Good struggling depends on a safe space, appropriately pitched challenge, links to prior learning, time to practise and an outcome that seems worthwhile.
Beginners need considerable support, and impatient teachers or parents can turn a good struggle into a bad one.
When Skelton observes lessons, the first thing he looks for is students who cannot yet but are engaged in the struggle.
Being a beginner is uncomfortable, so learning-focused adults must make that stage acceptable and even enjoyable.
quotes: Ximena, Liam, Aarifa and Aki are showing us what New learning looks like when we see it in front of us. New learning almost always looks like a struggle, because it almost always is a struggle.

Looking at these four young people doing very different things, we can see one thing they have in common. They are all struggling right now, because they have little to fall back on. They are hesitant, occasionally frustrated, but (and this is good news) they are willing to at least keep trying.

The struggle is worth it when the space in which it is happening feels safe, when the task is challenging but not too challenging, when the new learning has some relationship to previous learning but is different from it, when there is time for practice to happen and when the eventual outcomes seem worth it. The good struggle is what enables me to want to keep going.
Even though the struggle is good, it needs a great deal of support. In fact, good struggling demands lots of support from the ‘teacher’, support that enables the learner to continue the struggle.

They give people lots of time and lots of practice. Like Aarifa’s’s teacher, they know that struggling is the opening to the learning process and they create a space in which struggling is acceptable.

Good struggling is the clue to me that students may be beginning to move from somewhere they haven’t yet been to somewhere they can get to. It is the sign that learning might be beginning to happen, that some neuronal chains are beginning to be created.

One of the things I most want to see when I look round a class is whether learning is beginning to happen. Finding good struggling happening in front of me is my first chance to check. Good struggling is the moment when learning might begin to happen.
